### Observed differences

- The elapsed time between consecutive completion events of A10 and A11 roughly doubled. In the earlier window these gaps averaged about 1.0 hour (median about 1.0; the middle half between about 0.9 and 1.1 hours); in the later window they averaged about 2.0 hours (median about 2.0; the middle half between about 1.8 and 2.2 hours) — a mean increase of about 0.98 hours. [TWAIT001]
- The whole distribution shifted upward rather than a few cases becoming extreme: the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles each rose by roughly 0.9–1.1 hours, while the spread grew only modestly (standard deviation about 0.17 to 0.35 hours). [TWAIT001]
- The difference rests on many observations — about 334 gaps in the earlier window and about 305 in the later one, out of 200 traces per window — and it is larger than in all but about 1 of 2,000 random re-splits of the pooled data. [TWAIT001]
- Participation in the A10→A11 sequence barely moved: the number of observed gaps fell by about 30 (roughly 9%), and no control-flow indicator qualified (0 items against about 0.26 expected by chance), so both activities still occur and follow one another at similar rates; what changed is the time between their completions. [TWAIT001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a timing change on the transition from A10 to A11: in the later window, the elapsed time between consecutive completions of A10 and A11 is about one hour longer than before, roughly doubling from about 1.0 to about 2.0 hours. [TWAIT001]

Supporting signs: in the time family, one item qualified against roughly 0.009 expected without a change — more than a hundred times the chance expectation — while the control-flow family produced none (0 against about 0.26), so the signal is specific to this gap rather than a global slowdown; the change is measured directly by the indicator, is consistent across all distribution components, and is backed by roughly 300 gap observations in each window with a difference larger than in all but about 1 of 2,000 random re-splits. [TWAIT001]

Limitations: TWAIT measures elapsed time between consecutive completion events, so the evidence cannot show whether the extra hour comes from waiting, processing or handover; and a compositional shift — a different mix of cases reaching the A10→A11 pair with longer gaps — that stays below the control-flow thresholds cannot be fully ruled out. [TWAIT001]

Other differences: none beyond the slight (about 9%) dip in the number of observed gaps noted above, which is within sampling variation given that no control-flow item qualified. [TWAIT001]
